entries.question: Do bad things happen to good people?
entries.summary: Habakkuk 1:4 and 1:13 complain that the wicked surround the righteous and devour those more righteous than themselves, and Hebrews 12:6 affirms that Yahweh chastens every son he receives. Proverbs 12:21, Proverbs 19:23, and 1 Peter 3:13 insist no evil happens to the just and ask rhetorically who could harm a follower of good. The retribution principle collides head-on with prophetic protest and pastoral realism.
entries.commentary:
This is yet another iteration of the act-consequence-versus-protest theology fault line that runs through the Hebrew Bible and bleeds into the New Testament. Proverbs 12:21 — lo-ye'unneh la-tsaddiq kol-aven, "no harm shall happen to the righteous" — is a pure retribution claim. The proverb tradition needs this to be true for its moral framework to hold. Proverbs 19:23 piles on with the same promise about fear of Yahweh producing immunity from evil.

Then Habakkuk shows up as the prophet who refuses to accept that retribution claim. Habakkuk 1:13 — "why do you look on the treacherous, and stay silent when the wicked swallows up the one more righteous than he?" — is a frontal refutation of the Proverbs principle. Francis Andersen's Anchor Bible commentary on Habakkuk treats the book as a sustained interrogation of divine justice, written from inside the experience of injustice. Habakkuk does not get the Proverbs answer; he gets the by-faith-the-righteous-shall-live answer (Habakkuk 2:4), which is essentially a deferral.

1 Peter 3:13 — "who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good?" — is rhetorical and is immediately followed in 3:14 by "but even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed." 1 Peter knows the rhetorical question doesn't quite work and walks it back within two verses. Hebrews 12:6 (quoting Proverbs 3:11-12) takes the opposite tack: yes, the righteous suffer, and that is precisely God's discipline of his children. Apologist harmonization (Schreiner on 1 Peter, Lane on Hebrews) typically uses Hebrews 12 to glue the disparate texts together — bad things happen to the righteous, but for them suffering is reframed as discipline rather than retribution.

This is a real harmonization within the canon, attempted by Hebrews itself. But it concedes that Proverbs 12:21 was wrong on its face. The proverb said no harm happens to the righteous; Hebrews says harm does happen but it is repurposed as discipline. Those are different claims. The canon resolves the contradiction by replacing the retribution principle with a discipline-of-sons theology, but it does so by overruling the proverb, not by reconciling it.

Verdict: real contradiction. The biblical authors themselves disagree on whether the righteous are protected from harm, and the New Testament partly admits this by reframing harm-to-the-righteous as divine discipline — which is a theological retreat from the original Proverbs claim, not a harmonization of it.

entries.question: Who (or what) is a ransom for the righteous?
entries.books_in_tension: Job, Proverbs, Isaiah, Matthew, Mark, Romans, 1 Timothy
entries.summary: The Bible offers at least four mutually incompatible answers to who or what serves as a ransom for the righteous. Proverbs 21:18 says the wicked are the ransom; the Synoptic ransom logion and the deutero-Pauline pastorals say Jesus is; Proverbs 13:8 says it's a man's riches; and a separate stream from Job, Isaiah, and Romans denies there are any righteous people for whom to pay a ransom in the first place. The four claims do not reconcile because they presuppose different anthropologies and different economies of substitution.
entries.commentary:
Start with the Proverbs answer, because it's the one the apologists work hardest to bury. Proverbs 21:18 says the wicked (rasha) are a kopher — a ransom-price — for the righteous (tsaddiq). That's a wisdom-tradition retribution principle: the wicked get swapped in to absorb the disaster that would otherwise fall on the righteous. Bruce Waltke in the NICOT Proverbs commentary takes the line at face value as a Tun-Ergehen-Zusammenhang formula — deeds-have-consequences — where the wicked literally function as the substitute. No Christ in sight, no atonement theology, just folk-wisdom about cosmic accounting. Then jump eight chapters back to Proverbs 13:8 and the answer flips: it's your riches that ransom you. Michael Fox in the AYB volume reads this as straight wisdom-pragmatism — wealth buys you out of trouble — and notes the tension with 13:8b, where the poor man doesn't even hear the threat. The book contradicts itself within its own corpus.

The New Testament has its own ransom theology that has nothing to do with either Proverbs verse. Mark 10:45 and its Matthean parallel use lytron anti pollon — a ransom in exchange for many — and the apologist playbook page one is to harmonize this with Isaiah 53's suffering servant. Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark commentary documents the Greco-Roman manumission background: lytron is the price paid to free a slave. Jesus is the ransom, not the wicked, not riches. The pastoral 2 Timothy 2:6 (the SAB cites it but the actual ransom-for-all verse is 1 Timothy 2:6 — antilytron hyper panton; this looks like a scrape-side miscite worth flagging) extends ransom universally. So now the ransom is for all, not just the righteous, and it's paid by God-in-Christ, not collected from the wicked.

Now the fourth answer demolishes the question itself. Job 15:14, Isaiah 64:6, Romans 3:10 — the strand the Reformers loved — says nobody is righteous. If there are no righteous, the Proverbs 21:18 transaction has no beneficiary. Doug Moo in the NICNT Romans points out that Paul's catena in Romans 3:10-18 is precisely designed to deny the wisdom-tradition's tsaddiq/rasha binary. Paul is contradicting Proverbs to set up justification by faith. That's not me reading a contradiction in; that's the structure of the argument.

The harmonization attempt — "different senses of righteous" or "different covenantal contexts" — collapses on inspection. Proverbs is operating in a wisdom-tradition retribution frame; the Synoptics in an apocalyptic substitutionary frame; Paul in a forensic-imputation frame; Qohelet-adjacent strands in a no-one-deserves-anything frame. Those are four different theologies of how guilt and innocence get balanced. Take your pick — but you can't have all four without the whole thing breaking.

entries.question: Should we believe everything?
entries.summary: Paul's hymn to love in 1 Corinthians 13:7 says love 'believes all things,' but Proverbs 14:15, Proverbs 26:25, 1 Thessalonians 5:21, and 1 John 4:1 issue blanket commands to test, scrutinize, and not believe everyone or every spirit. The tension is between a credulity-as-virtue ethic and a verify-everything ethic, and it sits inside the Pauline corpus itself.
entries.commentary:
The apologist move here is to claim 1 Corinthians 13:7's panta pisteuei isn't about epistemic credulity at all — it's love's posture of hopeful trust toward the beloved. Anthony Thiselton in the NIGTC Corinthians commentary makes that case at length: pisteuei here is paired with elpizei and hypomenei, and the whole stanza is rhetorical-poetic, not an evidence-evaluation rubric. That's the best version of the harmonization, and it's not nothing.

But the problem is that the verse is exactly as ambiguous as it sounds. The Greek panta pisteuei reads on its face as 'believes all things' — and the Vulgate, the KJV, and centuries of devotional reading took it that way. Hans Conzelmann in the Hermeneia volume notes the deliberate hyperbole and the tension with Paul's own elsewhere-stated demand for discernment of spirits. So even on the steel-manned reading, what you've got is a poetic claim that love trusts maximally, set alongside a prophetic-wisdom tradition that says trusting maximally is how you get conned.

Proverbs 14:15 is the wisdom-tradition position in compressed form: the pethi — the simple, naive one — believes every word, and the prudent man looks where he's going. Michael Fox in the AYB volume reads this as a foundational wisdom contrast: credulity is moral immaturity, not virtue. 1 Thessalonians 5:21 — panta dokimazete — 'test all things' — is the same ethic translated into Pauline-community discourse, and 1 John 4:1's command to me panti pneumati pisteuete — 'do not believe every spirit' — is verbatim the negation of the Corinthians line, written by a different Johannine hand a generation or two later as community-discernment doctrine. Raymond Brown in the AB volume reads 1 John 4:1 as a direct response to schismatic prophecy claims; this is church discipline through epistemic skepticism.

The contradiction stands. You can soften 1 Cor 13:7 by reading it as hopeful rather than gullible, but you can't make the New Testament speak with one voice on whether the believer's default is trust or test. Paul says one thing in a hymn and another in a letter. Take your pick — the love-poem ethic that turns every Christian into an easy mark, or the discernment ethic that says verify before you commit.

entries.question: Does God want some to go to hell?
entries.books_in_tension: Proverbs, John, Romans, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, 2 Peter
entries.summary: 1 Timothy 2:3-4 and 2 Peter 3:9 say God wants every human saved; Proverbs 16:4, John 12:40, Romans 9:18-22, and 2 Thessalonians 2:11-12 portray a deity who creates the wicked for the day of evil, hardens hearts to prevent repentance, prepares vessels of wrath, and sends strong delusion so that the damned will be damned. The two strands of texts presuppose flatly different doctrines of the divine will.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction the Calvinist-Arminian fight has tried to paper over for five hundred years, and the fact that the fight is still going tells you the texts genuinely point in opposite directions. The pastoral and 2 Peter say what they say: God 'wills all men to be saved' (pantas anthropous thelei sothenai, 1 Tim 2:4), and the Lord is 'not willing that any should perish' (me boulomenos tinas apolesthai, 2 Pet 3:9). I. Howard Marshall in the ICC Pastoral Epistles reads this as a deliberate anti-elitist polemic against any incipient Christian gnosticism that wanted to restrict salvation to an elect — a universal-salvific-will is the point of the passage.

Then you turn to Romans 9. Doug Moo in the NICNT Romans and Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB volume both grant that Paul is constructing a hard-doctrine-of-divine-sovereignty argument: God 'has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens' (Rom 9:18), and the 'vessels of wrath prepared for destruction' language (9:22) is the apostle's deliberate invocation of potter-and-clay sovereignty from Jeremiah and Isaiah. James Dunn in the WBC Romans 9-16 treats the chapter as Paul's most uncompromising statement of unconditional election. John 12:40 explicitly cites Isaiah 6:10 — God blinded their eyes so they would not turn and be healed. That's a divine intention to prevent conversion. C. K. Barrett's Gospel According to St. John commentary doesn't flinch: the evangelist means what he wrote.

The apologist harmonization runs through a distinction between God's 'revealed will' (he commands repentance, wants all saved) and his 'decretive will' (he ordains who actually gets saved). Wayne Grudem and Norman Geisler both run this play, and within a tight systematic-theology frame it's internally consistent. But notice what the move costs: you have to say that when 1 Timothy says God 'wills all to be saved,' the word 'wills' (thelei) means something different from when Romans 9 says God 'has mercy on whom he wills' (hon thelei eleei). Same Greek verb, same author's tradition, opposite force. That is post-hoc rationalization with the receipts of post-hoc rationalization.

The more honest reading is the one the critical scholars have been giving for a century: the pastoral and 2 Peter belong to a late-NT universalizing strand reacting against sectarian exclusivism, while Paul and Johannine apocalyptic preserve an older predestinarian instinct rooted in Second-Temple Jewish determinism. Different authors, different communities, different theologies. The Bible doesn't have a unified doctrine of God's saving will. That is of course a critical judgment on the evidence, but the textual variation is not a translation artifact.

entries.question: If God likes you, will everyone else like you too?
entries.summary: Proverbs 16:7 promises that when a man's ways please YHWH, even his enemies will be at peace with him. 2 Timothy 3:12 says every single person who chooses to live godly in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. The wisdom-tradition assurance of social favor and the apocalyptic-Pauline expectation of inevitable persecution don't agree on what divine approval looks like in the world.
entries.commentary:
The Proverbs verse is wisdom-tradition orthodoxy in its most optimistic mode. Bruce Waltke in the NICOT volume reads 16:7 as a maxim from the Tun-Ergehen-Zusammenhang stable — please YHWH, and the social and political environment will reflect that pleasure back at you. Michael Fox in the AYB Proverbs notes that the wisdom-school context here is royal/courtly: if the king's ways please God, even foreign enemies sue for peace. That's the worldview. Walk in righteousness and the world cooperates with you.

2 Timothy operates in an entirely different theological universe. The pastoral is writing from inside a community that has just lived through Neronian-era hostility and Domitianic-era social marginalization. Pantes hoi thelontes eusebos zen — 'all who wish to live godly' — diochthesontai — 'will be persecuted.' I. Howard Marshall in the ICC Pastoral Epistles documents how 3:12 reads the entire history of suffering apostles as the normative pattern: persecution is not the exception, it's the proof. Luke Timothy Johnson in the AB Pastoral Epistles makes the same point — the suffering of the righteous is the apocalyptic frame the post-Pauline communities inherited from Second-Temple martyrology.

The apologist harmonization usually goes one of two ways. First move: 'enemies will be at peace' just means God preserves you — not that you'll have no enemies. Second move: the Proverbs verse is general wisdom, the 2 Timothy verse is specific Christian-era apocalyptic. Both moves work only if you're willing to gut Proverbs 16:7 of its surface claim. Roland Murphy in the WBC Proverbs already noted decades ago that the wisdom-tradition retribution principle is consistently undercut by Job and Qohelet from inside the wisdom corpus itself — the Hebrew Bible knows perfectly well that righteous people get hammered. So the contradiction isn't an artifact of misreading Proverbs against Paul; it's a contradiction Proverbs is having with itself, and 2 Timothy just lands on the opposite end of the same intra-biblical fight.

The verdict is straightforward. Proverbs 16:7 represents a hopeful retributive theology where divine approval shows up as social peace; 2 Timothy 3:12 represents an apocalyptic-martyrological theology where divine approval shows up as the cross. They're not reconcilable claims about how God's favor manifests in human relationships. Take your pick.

entries.question: Is it good to be happy?
entries.summary: Proverbs 17:22 and Ecclesiastes 8:15 commend merriment as medicinal and as the best thing humans can do under the sun. Ecclesiastes 7:3-4 and Luke 6:25 reverse the valuation — sorrow is better than laughter, the wise heart is in the house of mourning, and woe to those who laugh now. Even Qohelet contradicts himself on this question, and Luke's Jesus piles on from the other direction.
entries.commentary:
The most interesting feature of this contradiction is that it lives inside a single biblical book. Qohelet says both. Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes volume documents at length how the book oscillates between carpe diem affirmations (2:24, 3:12-13, 5:18, 8:15, 9:7-10) and meditations on the moral seriousness of grief (1:18, 4:1-3, 7:1-4). Seow reads the tension as Qohelet's deliberate dialectic: pleasure is the best thing available, and pleasure is hollow. Both claims, simultaneously, by design. Tremper Longman in the NICOT volume gets to the same place by a different route, calling Qohelet's voice a 'frame narrator' wrestling with two theological postures the wisdom tradition couldn't synthesize.

Then there's Proverbs 17:22, which is the wisdom tradition in its sunniest mood. Michael Fox in the AYB Proverbs reads the lev sameah — merry heart — as proto-psychosomatic medicine: cheerful disposition produces physical wellbeing. It's the kind of claim you find in Egyptian Instruction literature and in much later Greek medical writing. The book of Proverbs likes happiness.

Luke 6:25 is operating in an apocalyptic-prophetic register that does not. Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke volume reads the woes-and-beatitudes structure as classic prophetic reversal-language: those who laugh now will mourn later precisely because the present age is upside-down. François Bovon in the Hermeneia Luke 1 volume frames the woe as deliberate inversion of Hellenistic eudaimonia — Jesus is attacking the comfortable presupposition that present happiness is a sign of divine favor. The verse isn't poetry. It's eschatological reversal: enjoy your laughter now, the kingdom is coming and the ledger is going to be balanced.

The apologist harmonization runs through 'different kinds of happiness' — worldly mirth vs. spiritual joy, frivolous laughter vs. mature contentment. Apologetic commentators have run this distinction hard. But Qohelet uses the same Hebrew root (smḥ) for the merriment he praises and the laughter he mocks; Luke uses the same Greek root (gelao) for the laughter that will become mourning. The vocabulary isn't doing the work the harmonization needs it to do. You're left with a wisdom tradition that says be happy, a wisdom tradition that says don't be too happy, and a Jesus tradition that says happiness now is a downpayment on woe. The Bible doesn't speak with one voice on whether human happiness is good.

entries.question: What's new?
entries.summary: Ecclesiastes 1:9 says nothing is new under the sun and nothing ever will be. Isaiah 43:19 and 65:17, 2 Corinthians 5:17, 2 Peter 3:13, and Revelation 21:1 all announce that God is making new things, new creations, new heavens, and a new earth. The Qohelet-Stoic cyclical worldview and the apocalyptic-eschatological new-creation worldview run on opposite metaphysics.
entries.commentary:
Qohelet's 1:9 — 'there is nothing new under the sun' (ein kol chadash tachat hashemesh) — is the doctrinal anchor of the whole book's cyclical pessimism. Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes volume reads this as classic Hellenistic-era resignation literature: the world runs in repeating loops, history doesn't progress, what looks novel is just the same patterns recombining. Longman in the NICOT puts it bluntly: Qohelet's worldview is anti-eschatological. There is no breakthrough coming, no rupture, no new thing.

Isaiah 43:19 and 65:17 say exactly the opposite. Hineni oseh chadashah — 'behold, I am doing a new thing' — is Second Isaiah's announcement of a coming intervention so categorically novel that the old categories won't survive. Joseph Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 40-55 volume documents how the chadash language in Deutero-Isaiah is deliberately polemical against ancient Near Eastern cyclical cosmology — YHWH disrupts cycles. Third Isaiah's 65:17 escalates this to cosmic scale: new heavens and a new earth, with the old ones not even remembered. Blenkinsopp's AB Isaiah 56-66 reads this as proto-apocalyptic — the seedbed of the genre that Revelation will later inherit.

The New Testament rolls in the same direction. Victor Paul Furnish in the AB II Corinthians reads 2 Cor 5:17 — kaine ktisis, new creation — as Paul's most condensed statement of inaugurated eschatology. Richard Bauckham in the WBC 2 Peter and David Aune in the WBC Revelation 17-22 trace the Isaianic new-heavens-new-earth language straight into the apocalyptic finale. The eschatological strand of the Bible is built on the premise that newness is precisely what God specializes in.

The apologist response usually runs: Qohelet was speaking of nothing new under the natural order, while the prophets speak of supernatural new acts of God. Tremper Longman makes a version of this move, and to be fair, it's a plausible reading — 'under the sun' could be a register-restriction. But the harmonization doesn't survive contact with the actual texts. Qohelet 1:9 frames its claim universally — kol chadash, 'any new thing' — and the cyclical examples in 1:5-7 are cosmic, not merely sublunar. Qohelet is denying eschatology as a category. The apocalyptic strand depends on the category Qohelet denies. The contradiction is between two competing Jewish theologies of time: one wisdom-Hellenistic and cyclical, the other prophetic-apocalyptic and rupturalist. The Bible contains both, and they don't agree.

entries.question: Does hell exist?
entries.books_in_tension: Deuteronomy, Joshua, Job, Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, Daniel, Obadiah, Wisdom, 1 Maccabees, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 2 Thessalonians, 1 Timothy, Hebrews, James, 1 John, Jude, Revelation
entries.summary: The Bible offers four mutually incompatible afterlife schemes. The apocalyptic strand (Daniel 12, Matthew, Mark, Luke, 2 Thessalonians, Hebrews, Jude, Revelation) describes eternal conscious torment. The annihilationist strand (Psalms, Proverbs, Obadiah, Romans, Galatians, Philippians, James) describes the wicked being destroyed, perishing, and ceasing to exist. The universalist strand (1 Cor 15:22, 1 Tim 4:10, 1 John 2:2) has all humans made alive in Christ. And the Sheol-only strand (Job, Psalms, Qohelet, Isaiah 38) has everyone going to the same silent dust regardless of moral state. Critical scholarship reads this as four overlapping historical layers, not one coherent doctrine.
entries.commentary:
This is the contradiction that makes the most theological mileage, because the four positions are each defended by living religious communities — eternal-conscious-torment by traditional evangelicals and Catholics, annihilationism by conditionalists like Edward Fudge and a growing slice of evangelical scholars, universalism by figures like David Bentley Hart and Robin Parry, and the Sheol-only / no-afterlife reading by critical scholarship of the Hebrew Bible. Each side has the receipts because each set of texts genuinely says what those communities claim it says.

Start with the no-afterlife strand, because the apologist playbook page one is to pretend it doesn't exist. Job 7:9, Job 14:10-14, Ecclesiastes 3:19-21, Ecclesiastes 9:5-6, Psalm 6:5, Psalm 88:5, Psalm 115:17, Isaiah 38:18 — these are not isolated outliers. James Crenshaw in the OTL Ecclesiastes and Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes both treat Qohelet's denial of post-mortem reward as the book's foundational anthropology. Jon Levenson in *Resurrection and the Restoration of Israel* documents how the pre-exilic and early post-exilic Hebrew Bible has no developed afterlife — Sheol is just the grave-shadow, the same for everyone. The apocalyptic resurrection of Daniel 12 is, on Levenson's reading, a late innovation responding to Maccabean martyrdom. John Collins in the Hermeneia Daniel commentary nails the date: Daniel 12:2 is the first unambiguous biblical reference to differential post-mortem destinies, and it's from the 160s BCE.

Then the eternal-torment strand. Dale Allison in the ICC Matthew documents at length how Matthean apocalyptic deploys Gehenna imagery from Isaiah 66:24 and 1 Enoch to portray actual unending punishment. Joel Marcus on Mark 9:43-48 in the AYB doesn't soften the imagery — the worm that doesn't die and the fire that isn't quenched are deliberately permanent. David Aune in the WBC Revelation 17-22 reads the lake-of-fire torment 'forever and ever' (eis tous aionas ton aionon) as as strong as Greek can make the duration claim. So the apocalyptic strand is real, and it's not the sole property of medieval imagination.

Then the annihilationist strand, which uses the verbs the eternal-torment crowd would prefer to soften. Apollymi (perish), phtheiro (destroy), olethros (destruction) — these are destruction-words, and the texts say what they say. Edward Fudge in *The Fire That Consumes* and Glenn Peoples have made the conditionalist case from a confessionally evangelical position; you don't have to go to atheists for it. Romans 6:23 says the wages of sin is death, not eternal torment. 2 Thessalonians 1:9 says olethron aionion — eternal destruction — which conditionalists read as 'permanent destruction' (the result is eternal, not the process). Then the universalist strand — 1 Cor 15:22's 'in Adam all die, in Christ all shall be made alive' (pantes zōopoiēthēsontai) — has Origen and the Cappadocians arguing apokatastasis is the actual New Testament eschatology. David Bentley Hart's *That All Shall Be Saved* re-litigates the Greek and makes the case that eternal torment isn't even in the Pauline letters.

The harmonization attempts boil down to assigning different texts to different vocabularies — Sheol means the grave but not the soul, perishing means losing relationship not existence, universalist verses are about potential not actual scope. Each move can be defended in isolation, but the combined harmonization requires four different translation conventions enforced selectively. The honest critical reading is the developmental one: the Hebrew Bible mostly has no afterlife, the late Second Temple period imports differential post-mortem destinies from Persian and Hellenistic sources, early Christianity carries forward the apocalyptic version, and the universalist and annihilationist strands are minority readings that survived inside the canon. The Bible doesn't teach a single doctrine of hell. Take your pick — which is exactly what every Christian tradition has been doing for two thousand years.

entries.question: Is money good or bad?
entries.summary: Ecclesiastes 10:19 says money answers all things — every problem in life has a financial solution. 1 Timothy 6:10 says the love of money is the root of all evil. One is wisdom-tradition pragmatism about wealth's utility; the other is Hellenistic-Jewish moralism about wealth's spiritual danger.
entries.commentary:
The apologist move on this one is to point out that 1 Timothy 6:10 doesn't say money is the root of all evil — it says philargyria, the love of money, is. That's correct as far as it goes. The KJV's 'love of money is the root of all evil' is technically accurate, even if the indefinite-article rendering 'a root of all kinds of evils' (NRSV, NA28) softens it slightly. Luke Timothy Johnson in the AB Pastoral Epistles documents that philargyria was a stock Hellenistic moralist topos — the same Greek term shows up in Diogenes Laertius and Polybius as a fundamental vice. So 1 Timothy 6:10 is doing standard Greco-Roman ethics: greed corrupts.

But Ecclesiastes 10:19 isn't saying anything about greed. Qohelet says ha-kesef yaaneh et ha-kol — silver answers all. Choon-Leong Seow in the AB Ecclesiastes reads this as Qohelet's characteristic dark realism: money is the universal solvent of human problems, full stop. Not 'money has its dangers but useful in moderation' — money answers everything. Tremper Longman in the NICOT volume notes that Qohelet's claim is being made within a book that is otherwise quite ready to denounce the hoarding of wealth (5:10-17), so 10:19 is a deliberately unsentimental observation about how money actually functions in the social world.

The harmonization usually goes through carve-outs: Ecclesiastes is describing how things are; 1 Timothy is describing how things should be. That's a fair reading and it does relieve some of the tension. But notice what it concedes — Qohelet is teaching that the actual, real-world function of wealth is to answer all problems, and the Christian moral tradition is telling you to repudiate that exact attitude. The Bible contains both the cynical pragmatism and the moralistic warning. Whether that counts as 'contradiction' or 'tension within a multi-voiced canon' depends on how charitable you want to be about canonical pluralism. The critical reading is that the wisdom-pragmatist strand and the apocalyptic-moralist strand have always pulled in opposite directions on wealth, and the Bible never resolves the fight — it just lets both voices speak.

entries.question: Who is the first and the last?
entries.summary: Isaiah 48:12 — and 41:4, 44:6 — has YHWH declaring 'I am the first and the last.' Revelation 1:17 and 22:13 have Jesus saying the same thing. Either the title applies to two distinct entities, in which case it's a contradiction, or Jesus is being identified with YHWH, in which case the contradiction dissolves into Christology and creates a different problem with strict monotheism.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the contradictions the apologist can hand-wave in two directions, and we should give both directions their due. Path one: Jesus and the Father are the same God, so 'first and last' applying to both is just the doctrine of the Trinity in compressed form. Path two: 'first and last' applies in different senses — to YHWH cosmically and to Jesus as the first-born of the new creation. Both moves have ancient pedigree. Richard Bauckham in *Jesus and the God of Israel* argues that Revelation's deliberate transfer of Isaianic divine titles to Jesus is exactly the strategy by which early Christians included Jesus in the unique identity of YHWH without compromising monotheism.

But you can't get Bauckham's resolution for free. Notice what it costs. Deutero-Isaiah's whole rhetorical strategy in 44:6-8 and 48:12 is to insist that there is no other deity — ani rishon va-ani acharon u-mibal'aday ein elohim, 'I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no god.' Joseph Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 40-55 reads these declarations as polemical anti-Babylonian monotheism: Marduk doesn't exist, Bel doesn't exist, only YHWH. The exclusivity is the point. When Revelation 1:17 and 22:13 — and 22:13 explicitly adds 'the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end' — picks up that vocabulary for Jesus, the Apocalypse is either identifying Jesus with the one-and-only YHWH (Bauckham's reading) or it's compromising Isaiah's exclusive monotheism. David Aune in the WBC Revelation 1-5 and Revelation 17-22 documents the deliberate Christological appropriation and notes the theological cost.

The critical scholarship reading is the developmental one: Isaiah's strict monotheism is what late Second-Temple Judaism inherited; early Christian Christology had to do something with the resurrection-exaltation tradition and the increasingly elevated Jesus-language in Paul, Hebrews, and Revelation; the result is what Larry Hurtado called 'binitarian' devotion — two figures, both somehow divine, in a tradition that nominally remained monotheistic. Daniel Boyarin in *Border Lines* argues this was always less stable than later orthodoxy admitted, and Margaret Barker has gone further in *The Great Angel* arguing that pre-rabbinic Judaism already had two-power traditions that Christianity inherited. The SAB framing as 'contradiction' is a fair surface read. The harmonization through trinitarianism works only if you grant the entire Nicene framework; without it, Revelation is straightforwardly transferring YHWH-titles to a second figure, and Isaiah said that wasn't supposed to be possible. Take your pick.

entries.question: What was Sodom's sin?
entries.books_in_tension: Genesis, Leviticus, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Wisdom, Matthew, Luke, 2 Peter, Jude
entries.summary: The Bible names at least six different sins as the reason Sodom was destroyed: same-sex intercourse (Leviticus 18:22 read into Ezekiel 16:50), inhospitality (Matthew 10, Luke 10, Wisdom 19:13), seeking sex with angels and 'strange flesh' (Genesis 19, Jude 7), pride and neglect of the poor (Isaiah 1, Ezekiel 16:49), adultery and lying (Jeremiah 23:14), and generic ungodliness (2 Peter 2). The 'homosexuality' reading is a late interpretive overlay that the Hebrew Bible's own internal cross-references don't support.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleanest examples in the canon of an interpretive trajectory overwriting the source text. Genesis 19 records a mob demanding to 'know' (yada) two angelic visitors at Lot's house. The verb yada in Hebrew has a sexual sense in a minority of its 943 occurrences, but the demand context here makes a sexual reading defensible. What the verb does not specify is that the sin is the same-sex orientation of the act rather than the gang-rape-of-foreigners structure of it. Susan Niditch in *Judges* (OTL) and Phyllis Trible in *Texts of Terror* both document how the Genesis 19 / Judges 19 parallel — the Gibeah outrage — is structurally about violation of guest-rights through sexual violence, not about same-sex desire as such.

More decisively: when the Hebrew Bible looks back at Sodom, it does not name same-sex intercourse. Ezekiel 16:49 lists Sodom's iniquity in order — pride, surfeit of bread, prosperous ease, failure to aid the poor and needy. Walther Zimmerli in the Hermeneia Ezekiel 1 commentary takes this list at face value: the prophetic indictment of Sodom is socioeconomic and theological, not sexual in the modern sense. Verse 50 adds 'they did toevah before me' — and toevah is a wide-spectrum abomination term that the apologist crowd reads as referring to Leviticus 18:22, but which Zimmerli notes more naturally refers to the cumulative arrogance just listed. Isaiah 1:10-17 makes the same point with the same emphasis: the 'rulers of Sodom' are corrupt judges who oppress the widow and the orphan. Jeremiah 23:14 cites Sodom for adultery and lying among the prophets. The OT trajectory is consistent and it isn't about homosexuality.

The Synoptic Jesus follows that trajectory. Matthew 10:14-15 and Luke 10:10-12 cite Sodom as the type-case of inhospitality — the rejection of God's messengers — and Wisdom 19:13-17, written in Greek-speaking Jewish Alexandria, makes this completely explicit: Sodom's sin was that they 'practiced a more bitter hatred of strangers.' That's the inherited interpretation through at least the first century CE.

The shift happens with Jude 7's 'strange flesh' (sarkos heteras) and the Second Temple para-biblical literature — 1 Enoch 6-11, Jubilees 16, the Testament of Naphtali — where Sodom gets read through the Watchers-Genesis 6 lens of human-angel sexual transgression. Richard Bauckham in the WBC Jude / 2 Peter documents this trajectory with care. The Jude reading is angelic-sex transgression, not human same-sex orientation. The further shift to 'homosexuality' is a medieval and early modern Christian retrojection, securely placed by John Boswell in *Christianity, Social Tolerance, and Homosexuality* and more recently by Bernadette Brooten in *Love Between Women*.

The critical reading is straightforward: Sodom's sin in the Hebrew Bible and its first-century inheritors is pride, social oppression, and inhospitality; in the Second Temple apocalyptic tradition it expands to include forbidden angel-flesh crossing; the modern 'homosexuality' reading is anachronistic. The SAB framing as 'contradiction' is correct on the surface but undersells the more interesting point — the biblical authors knew what Sodom's sin was, and it wasn't what twentieth-century preachers said it was.

entries.question: What was Jesus H. Christ's real name?
entries.books_in_tension: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John, Revelation
entries.summary: The New Testament gives Jesus a long string of names and titles — Jesus, Jesus Christ, Emmanuel, the Word, Son of Man, Son of the Highest, Son of David, Son of God, Holy One of God, Lord Our Righteousness, Alpha and Omega, the Amen, Lion of Judah, Faithful and True, Word of God, King of Kings, the Morning Star, Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace — and Revelation 19:12 says no one knows his real name at all. The 'contradiction' as posed is largely a category error (these are titles, not legal names), but the underlying problem — competing Christological titles drawn from different prophetic streams — is real.
entries.commentary:
The SAB's framing is half-joke, half-serious, and the joke shouldn't obscure the serious half. As a question about Jesus's actual legal name, the answer is boring: Yeshua bar Yosef of Nazareth, a Galilean Jew who probably went by Yeshu in everyday Aramaic. That's the position John P. Meier defends in *A Marginal Jew* and Dale Allison in *Constructing Jesus* — historical, mundane, no controversy. Jesus is the Latinized Greek of the Hebrew Yehoshua/Yeshua. Christ is a title (mashiach / christos, 'anointed one'), not a surname. Emmanuel ('God-with-us') is a programmatic title Matthew imports from Isaiah 7:14, not a name Jesus's friends actually called him.

Where the question becomes scholarly-interesting is in the proliferation of Christological titles across the New Testament. Larry Hurtado in *Lord Jesus Christ* and Martin Hengel in *Studies in Early Christology* document how the earliest Jesus communities accumulated titles from multiple Jewish prophetic and apocalyptic streams: the Davidic Messiah (Son of David, Lion of Judah), the apocalyptic Son of Man (Daniel 7), the Mosaic Prophet, the Suffering Servant of Isaiah 53, the pre-existent Wisdom-Logos of John 1, the divine throne-sharer of Daniel 7 and Psalm 110, the divine warrior of Revelation. Each title carried its own theological freight. Calling Jesus 'Son of David' makes a different claim than calling him 'the Word.' Calling him 'the Lion of Judah' makes a different claim than calling him 'the Lamb that was slain.' Raymond Brown in *An Introduction to New Testament Christology* maps this title-by-title and shows how the assemblage doesn't form a unified Christological system — it forms a set of overlapping vocabularies the early church found useful for different rhetorical purposes.

Revelation 19:12 — 'he had a name written that no one knew but he himself' — and 22:16's 'morning star' are doing apocalyptic-mystery work that doesn't sit comfortably with the very next verse identifying him as 'the Word of God.' David Aune in the WBC Revelation 17-22 reads 19:12 as deliberate magical-name-theology, drawing on ancient Near Eastern and Greco-Roman ideas that knowing a divinity's secret name confers power; that's why John has Jesus retain a hidden name even as the surface text piles up public titles. Even within Revelation itself, the seer can't decide whether Jesus's true name is known or unknown.

The Isaiah 9:6 entry — Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace — adds a complication. Joseph Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 1-39 reads the verse as an enthronement-oracle for a Davidic king, possibly Hezekiah, with the throne-names being honorifics in the Egyptian style. The Christian reading projects all of this onto Jesus retrospectively. So even granting the Christological appropriation, you've got a 'name' that originally belonged to an Iron Age Judean king getting transferred to a first-century Galilean. The SAB question is a joke, but the underlying historical-critical observation — early Christianity assembled Jesus's identity from a portfolio of pre-existing prophetic-royal titles — is exactly right.

entries.question: Will the Messiah be a descendant of David?
entries.summary: Isaiah 11:1 and Jeremiah 23:5-6 promise a Davidic messiah — a Branch from David's line who will reign as king. In Mark 12:35-37, Jesus quotes Psalm 110 and argues that the Messiah cannot be David's son because David himself calls him 'Lord.' The Synoptic Jesus is denying the very Davidic-descent expectation that the prophets and the genealogies of Matthew and Luke spent so much energy establishing.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the contradictions where the New Testament is genuinely at war with itself. Matthew 1 and Luke 3 supply elaborate (and mutually incompatible) genealogies establishing Jesus's Davidic descent. Romans 1:3 calls Jesus 'descended from David according to the flesh.' Revelation 5:5 calls him 'the Root of David.' The Davidic-messiah expectation in Second Temple Judaism is documented exhaustively — John Collins in *The Scepter and the Star* shows that the Psalms of Solomon 17, the Qumran 4Q174 Florilegium, and the Sibylline Oracles all expected an actual biological descendant of David.

Then Mark 12:35-37 has Jesus standing in the temple and asking — pos legousin hoi grammateis hoti ho christos huios estin Dauid — 'how do the scribes say that the Messiah is the son of David?' He quotes Psalm 110:1 (LXX 109:1): the Lord said to my Lord, sit at my right hand. If David calls him Lord, Jesus argues, how is he his son? The rhetorical force of the question implies the messiah is not David's son — he's David's Lord, someone above David in the cosmic hierarchy. Joel Marcus in the AYB Mark 8-16 reads this pericope as a deliberate problematizing of the Davidic-descent tradition, possibly reflecting an early christology in which the post-resurrection enthronement (Psalm 110) mattered more than biological lineage. Adela Yarbro Collins in the Hermeneia Mark gets to the same conclusion: the Markan Jesus is challenging the messianic paradigm the scribes assumed.

The apologist harmonization usually runs through two paths. Path one: Jesus isn't denying he's David's son; he's pointing out that 'son of David' isn't sufficient — he's also more than that, a divine figure exalted above David. Craig Evans in the WBC Mark 8:27-16:20 makes this case at length. Path two: the genealogies in Matthew and Luke establish legal descent through Joseph, while the Markan pericope is pointing toward a higher Christology that's compatible with that legal descent. Both paths have textual support, and they're not absurd readings.

But here's the problem. The Markan question is rhetorical, and the rhetorical force depends on the conclusion that the Messiah is not the son of David. If Jesus is okay with also being David's son, the question doesn't work — David would just be addressing his future descendant in advance, and there's no scandal in calling one's distant scion 'Lord.' The Markan logic only sings if the Davidic-descent expectation is being challenged. And then the Pauline 'descended from David according to the flesh' and the Matthean and Lukan genealogies are doing the opposite work. The simplest critical reading is that the early Christian movement contained both an exaltation-Christology that didn't need Davidic biology and a Davidic-Messiah Christology that did, and the canon preserves both without reconciling them. Take your pick — Jesus the Davidic king, or Jesus the pre-existent Lord whose David-descent the Markan polemic was already trying to relativize.

entries.question: Will everyone see the majesty of God?
entries.summary: Isaiah 40:5 declares that the glory of YHWH will be revealed and all flesh — kol basar — will see it together. Isaiah 26:10, four chapters into the so-called 'Isaiah Apocalypse,' says the wicked will not behold the majesty of YHWH. The two declarations sit fourteen chapters apart in the same book, and the contradiction is internal to Isaiah.
entries.commentary:
The two verses come from radically different compositional layers of Isaiah, and recognizing that solves nothing and clarifies everything. Isaiah 40:5 is the opening oracle of Deutero-Isaiah, addressed to exiles in Babylon in the late sixth century BCE. Joseph Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 40-55 reads kol basar yachdav — all flesh together — as deliberately universal, contrasted with the Babylonian gods who reveal themselves only to initiates. The point is unrestricted visibility: even Gentiles, even pagans, will see YHWH's glory. Klaus Baltzer in the Hermeneia Deutero-Isaiah pushes the universalism even further, reading the verse as proto-eschatological theophany — the day comes when nobody is excluded from witnessing the divine kabod.

Isaiah 26:10 sits inside the Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24-27), a later, post-exilic apocalyptic block. The verse declares that the rasha — the wicked one — yuchan rasha bal-lamad tsedeq — even when favored, will not learn righteousness, and bal-yireh ge'ut YHWH — will not see the majesty of YHWH. Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 1-39 and Otto Kaiser in the OTL Isaiah 13-39 both date this material to the late Persian or early Hellenistic period and read it as classical apocalyptic differentiation: the righteous will see, the wicked will not. The eschatological visibility is sorted by moral category.

So what you've got is Deutero-Isaiah's universalist theophany running into the Isaiah Apocalypse's morally sorted theophany. The apologist harmonization — 'all flesh will see in some sense, but only the righteous will truly behold' — is doing what apologetic harmonizations always do: introducing a distinction the text doesn't make. kol basar yachdav doesn't admit of subdivision; bal-yireh ge'ut YHWH doesn't admit of partial vision. The verses are talking past each other because their authors had different theologies of revelation.

More broadly, this is an exhibit for why source-critical analysis of Isaiah matters. Bernhard Duhm's 1892 division into First, Second, and Third Isaiah — refined a century later by Brevard Childs, Hugh Williamson, and Blenkinsopp — produces compositional layers that disagree with each other on basic theological questions. The book Isaiah is not a single author's coherent doctrine; it's a multi-century anthology that has been redacted to look like a unity. The SAB question is correct to spot the contradiction. The critical-scholarly explanation is that two different sixth-and-fifth century BCE authors put incompatible eschatologies in the same scroll, and the editors didn't smooth them out.

entries.question: Does God ever get furious?
entries.summary: Isaiah 27:4 has YHWH declare 'fury is not in me' (chemah ein li). At least seven other texts across the prophetic and apocalyptic corpus — Isaiah 34:2, Jeremiah 7:20, Jeremiah 21:5, Jeremiah 30:23, Micah 5:15, Nahum 1:2, Zechariah 8:2 — describe YHWH as repeatedly, often, and copiously furious. Isaiah 27:4 is sitting seven chapters away from Isaiah 34:2 contradicting itself within the same scroll.
entries.commentary:
The Isaiah 27:4 verse is contextually difficult and the apologist will lean on that first. The verse comes inside the so-called Vineyard Song redux (Isa 27:2-6), and the Hebrew of 27:4a is genuinely ambiguous — chemah ein li, 'wrath/fury is not to me/in me.' Some translations render this as 'I am not angry,' others as 'I have no wrath' in the limited sense of 'against my vineyard.' Joseph Blenkinsopp in the AB Isaiah 1-39 notes the textual difficulty and reads the verse as a conditional disclaimer: YHWH has no wrath against Israel-as-vineyard, but plenty of wrath available for the briers and thorns the next verse threatens to burn. So the verse, in context, isn't claiming YHWH is wrathless in general — it's claiming YHWH is currently disposed toward protective rather than punitive action toward Israel.

That's the steel-man, and it's a reasonable contextual reading. But the SAB's framing isn't entirely defeated by it, because the verse on its surface — and as quoted in any English translation a lay reader encounters — does say 'fury is not in me' with no asterisk. Brevard Childs in the OTL Isaiah and Otto Kaiser in the OTL Isaiah 13-39 both note the verse's tension with the broader Isaianic portrayal of YHWH's wrath, which Childs reads as a deliberate inner-Isaianic theological tension between a wrathful God and a salvific God in tension across the book's compositional layers.

The contradicting texts are unambiguous. Isaiah 34:2 has YHWH's chemah (the same word as 27:4) poured out on all the armies of the nations. Jeremiah's chemah and aph language is so dense Jack Lundbom in the AB Jeremiah devotes substantial commentary to documenting Jeremiah's portrait of an enraged deity. Nahum 1:2 — 'YHWH is a jealous and avenging God; YHWH avenges and is full of wrath' — is the prophetic-poetic apex of divine fury. K.-D. Schunck in the TDOT volume on chemah catalogs the noun's over 100 occurrences and notes that the overwhelming majority depict actual divine rage. So whether the contradiction is intra-Isaianic (chemah ein li in 27:4 vs. we-chemah al-kol-tseva'am in 34:2) or inter-prophetic (Isa 27:4 vs. Jeremiah, Micah, Nahum, Zechariah), it's there.

The broader theological point — and this is where critical scholarship adds something the apologetic frame can't — is that the Hebrew Bible's portrayal of YHWH's emotional life is multi-vocal precisely because different prophetic strands had different working theologies of divine pathos. Abraham Heschel's *The Prophets* documented this with care: the prophetic God is not a passionless metaphysical absolute but a covenant-bound figure whose emotional state tracks Israel's behavior. The contradiction between Isaiah 27:4 and Nahum 1:2 isn't a Bible-versus-Bible puzzle to be solved; it's the Hebrew prophetic tradition's deliberate refusal to settle on a single doctrine of divine affect.

entries.question: Should you pray for everyone?
entries.summary: 1 Timothy 2:1 commands prayer and intercession for all people without exception. Jeremiah 7:16, 11:14, and 14:11 record YHWH explicitly forbidding Jeremiah from praying for the people of Judah — three times — because he will not hear. The pastoral universalism and the Jeremianic prohibition can't both be operative as standing divine commands.
entries.commentary:
Three times in Jeremiah, YHWH gives the prophet a direct command to stop praying. al-titpallel be'ad ha-am ha-zeh — 'do not pray for this people' (Jer 7:16, 11:14, 14:11). Jack Lundbom in the AB Jeremiah 1-20 treats the formula as one of the most striking elements of Jeremiah's vocation: the prophet is forbidden from doing the one thing prophets are normally expected to do, which is intercede for the covenant community. William Holladay in the Hermeneia Jeremiah 1-25 reads the prohibitions as marking the point of no return in the covenantal relationship — the people have crossed a threshold beyond which intercession is no longer permitted. This is severe stuff. It's not a casual narrative detail; it's a theological earthquake in the book of Jeremiah's understanding of when prayer works.

The pastoral 1 Timothy 2:1-4 reads as if Jeremiah doesn't exist. parakalo oun proton panton poieisthai deeseis, proseuchas, enteuxeis, eucharistias hyper panton anthropon — 'I urge that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people.' Luke Timothy Johnson in the AB Pastoral Epistles reads this as deliberate anti-sectarian universalism: the pastoral author is pushing back against any Christian community that would restrict its intercessory scope to insiders. I. Howard Marshall in the ICC Pastoral Epistles documents the rhetorical force — hyper panton anthropon, three times in three verses — and notes that this is meant to be programmatic, not aspirational.

The apologist harmonization is straightforward: the Jeremianic prohibition is situational and time-bound (specific to pre-exilic Judah at a specific moment), while 1 Timothy is a standing instruction. That's true as far as it goes, and Lundbom would partly agree with the situational framing. But the harmonization doesn't quite finish the job, because what 1 Timothy 2:1 establishes is that there is never a category of person you should refrain from praying for. The Jeremianic position presupposes the opposite: there are categories of person God has decided not to hear, and the prophet is not to waste prayer on them. Even granted the situational specificity, what Jeremiah teaches about prayer — there are circumstances in which intercession is futile — is the position 1 Timothy is denying. The contradiction is not at the level of any single prohibition; it's at the level of the underlying doctrine of intercession.

This matters because both texts have been read as theological warrants. Calvinist treatments of imprecatory psalms and reprobation lean on the Jeremianic strand. Catholic and broadly evangelical universal-intercession practice leans on 1 Timothy. Both Christian traditions have biblical receipts. That's the contradiction.

entries.question: Should we look for signs from heaven?
entries.summary: Luke 21:11 has Jesus predict that 'fearful sights and great signs from heaven' will accompany the eschaton, treating such signs as legitimate revelatory markers. Jeremiah 10:2 commands Israel not to be dismayed at the signs of heaven, because that's what the heathen do. One text validates celestial divination as eschatological evidence; the other condemns it as pagan superstition.
entries.commentary:
The Jeremiah 10:2 prohibition is part of an extended anti-idolatry polemic (10:1-16) that critical scholars often associate with Deutero-Jeremianic or post-exilic editorial layers. Robert Carroll in the OTL Jeremiah reads the passage as deliberate exilic-period polemic against Babylonian astral religion — the same celestial-omen practice that produced cuneiform sources like Enūma Anu Enlil. Jack Lundbom in the AB Jeremiah notes that otot ha-shamayim, 'signs of the heavens,' is technical Babylonian astrological vocabulary. The whole point of the verse is to distinguish Israel from its Mesopotamian neighbors by rejecting celestial divination as a religious practice. Don't read the stars, the verse says. That's gentile stuff.

Luke 21:11 is sitting at a completely different cultural moment. The Synoptic Apocalypse is drawing on Jewish apocalyptic traditions in which eschatological cosmic disturbances — earthquakes, eclipses, falling stars, plagues — are read as legitimate revelatory data. Joseph Fitzmyer in the AB Luke X-XXIV documents the literary background in Isaiah 13, Joel 2-3, and 1 Enoch, where celestial phenomena announce the day of YHWH. François Bovon in the Hermeneia Luke 3 reads Luke 21:11 as straightforward apocalyptic-tradition material, treating ap' ouranou sēmeia megala — great signs from heaven — as legitimate eschatological markers.

So the contradiction is at a level deeper than 'don't look at the sky' versus 'look at the sky.' It's a contradiction between an anti-divination strand of Israelite religion that wanted to distinguish Yahwistic faith from Babylonian astrology, and an apocalyptic strand that wholeheartedly adopted the same celestial-omen vocabulary because it had become useful for predicting the end times. James VanderKam in *Calendars in the Dead Sea Scrolls* and John Collins in *The Apocalyptic Imagination* both document how Jewish apocalyptic literature (Daniel, 1 Enoch, the Qumran scrolls) is saturated with cosmological signs the Jeremiah author would have considered idolatrous.

The apologist harmonization runs through distinguishing 'taking signs as omens for divinatory purposes' (forbidden) from 'recognizing signs that announce the eschaton' (encouraged). That's a real distinction — and one Christian commentators have made for centuries. But the distinction collapses when you notice that the eschaton-announcing signs in Luke 21 are functionally identical to the divinatory signs in Babylonian astrology: cosmic disturbances read as portents of regime change and divine action. The Lukan apocalypse has imported the technique the Jeremianic anti-idolatry polemic forbade. Take your pick — Jeremiah's anti-astral monotheism, or Luke's apocalyptic-cosmological semiotics.

entries.question: Will those who call on the Lord be delivered?
entries.books_in_tension: Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel, Micah, Matthew, Acts, Romans
entries.summary: Joel 2:32 — cited by Acts 2:21 and Romans 10:13 — promises that everyone who calls on the name of YHWH/Lord will be saved. Matthew 7:21, Jeremiah 14:12, Ezekiel 8:18, and Micah 3:4 describe categories of people who call on the Lord and are explicitly not heard, not saved, and not delivered. The unconditional Joel-Pauline promise runs into a thicket of conditional and rejection-language texts.
entries.commentary:
Joel 2:32 — kol asher yiqra beshem YHWH yimmalet, 'all who call on the name of YHWH will be delivered' — is one of the most universalist verses in the prophetic corpus. James Crenshaw in the AB Joel reads it as a deliberate expansion of salvation beyond ethnic Israel, prefiguring later inclusivist readings. Paul's two citations of it in Acts 2:21 (Pentecost sermon) and Romans 10:13 (the famous justification-by-faith chapter) lean on the verse's apparent unconditionality: anyone, no qualifications, whoever calls is saved. Doug Moo in the NICNT Romans documents how Romans 10:13 is the climactic prooftext for Paul's argument that the gospel is genuinely universal.

But Matthew 7:21 sees the same vocabulary and explicitly negates it. ou pas ho legon moi kyrie kyrie eiseleusetai eis ten basileian ton ouranon — 'not everyone who says to me Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven.' Dale Allison and W. D. Davies in the ICC Matthew read this as a deliberate intra-Christian polemic: the Matthean community is worried about confessors-without-works, and the verse is designed to deny that 'calling on the Lord' is by itself sufficient. Ulrich Luz in the Hermeneia Matthew 1-7 makes the same point — Matthew 7:21 is anti-charismatic-cheap-grace.

Then the prophetic rejection-texts. Jeremiah 14:12 — when they fast I will not hear their cry — comes from one of the prophet's intercession-prohibition passages discussed in the previous contradiction. Ezekiel 8:18 — though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not hear them — sits inside the temple-vision sequence where YHWH is leaving Jerusalem. Walther Zimmerli in the Hermeneia Ezekiel 1 documents the verse as part of the theological architecture justifying the exile: there comes a point when prayer doesn't work because the divine ear is closed. Micah 3:4 — then they shall cry to YHWH but he will not answer them — is straight prophetic-judgment formula.

The apologist resolution typically distinguishes two senses of 'calling.' Sincere calling with faith and repentance gets you delivered (Joel, Paul). Insincere or merely formal calling without underlying covenant fidelity gets you ignored (Matthew, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Micah). Walter Kaiser and others have run this distinction at length. It's a reasonable systematic-theology move, and it's not wrong. But notice what it costs the universalist reading. Joel 2:32 as cited by Paul in Romans 10 is doing rhetorical work that depends on its unconditionality — kol, pas, everyone. If you have to insert a faith-and-repentance qualifier, you're not citing Joel 2:32 anymore; you're citing 'Joel 2:32 plus the implicit conditions Matthew 7:21 supplies.' That's a synthesis, not a quotation.

The critical reading is the developmental one: Joel's late-prophetic universalism gets taken up by early Christianity as a gospel-of-grace prooftext, while the Matthean and prophetic-judgment strands preserve an older conditional theology in which divine hearing was always contingent on covenant fidelity. Different strata of the canon are working with different theologies of intercessory access. The Bible doesn't speak with one voice on whether prayer-as-such delivers, and the apologetic resolution requires you to read one passage through the implicit assumptions of another.

entries.question: How long was the Babylonian Captivity?
entries.summary: Jeremiah 25:11 and 29:10 set the Babylonian Captivity at seventy years. Baruch 6:2 — the Letter of Jeremiah — gives the duration as 'seven generations.' Even granting flexible generation-lengths, seventy years and seven generations are mathematically incompatible figures, and the historical-archaeological evidence makes both numbers schematic rather than literal.
entries.commentary:
Start with the actual historical chronology. The first Babylonian deportation under Nebuchadnezzar happened in 597 BCE; the destruction of the temple was 587/586 BCE; and the return under Cyrus's decree is conventionally dated to 538 BCE. So the captivity ran roughly 48 years from the destruction of the temple to the decree, or 59 years from the first deportation. Lester Grabbe in *A History of the Jews and Judaism in the Second Temple Period* does the math carefully and notes that the 'seventy years' of Jeremiah is already an approximation, not a hard count.

Where does the seventy come from? Jack Lundbom in the AB Jeremiah 21-36 documents the symbolic resonance: seventy is a round number in the Hebrew Bible (Israel's seventy nations, Moses's seventy elders, the seventy-week Daniel apocalypse), and it carries connotations of completion and divine ordering. The fact that the actual exile lasted roughly fifty years and Jeremiah rounds it to seventy is not a historical embarrassment — it's the prophet using a schematic number. William Holladay in the Hermeneia Jeremiah 1-25 reads the seventy-year figure as deliberate cosmological symbol, not chronicle.

Daniel 9 then extends and reinterprets Jeremiah's seventy years as seventy weeks of years, which is 490 years, which gets you from the exile down to the Maccabean crisis. John Collins in the Hermeneia Daniel makes the case decisively: Daniel 9 is a second-century BCE apocalyptic recalculation of an already-schematic Jeremianic number. So even within the Jewish canon, the seventy-year duration is being treated flexibly.

Baruch's Letter of Jeremiah (deuterocanonical Baruch 6, in the Vulgate's numbering — what Greek MSS call the Epistle of Jeremiah) sets the duration at seven generations. Carey A. Moore in the AB volume on Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah dates the work to roughly the late fourth or third century BCE and notes that 'seven generations' is itself a schematic figure derived from Genesis-style genealogical theology — seven is the perfection-number. A biblical generation is usually reckoned at 30-40 years, which gives a range of 210-280 years. That's not 70 years.

The apologist harmonization runs through several paths. Path one: maybe Baruch is talking about something different — a longer cultural exile rather than the strict political one. Path two: 'seven generations' is loose figurative language. Path three: the Letter of Jeremiah isn't canonical anyway (Protestant move), so the contradiction doesn't matter. All three moves have some traction, but they don't dissolve the underlying issue, which is that Second Temple Jewish literature contained multiple, incompatible schematizations of how long the exile was. Jeremiah says seventy years. Daniel says seventy weeks of years. Baruch says seven generations. Critical chronology says about fifty years from temple destruction to return. Lester Grabbe's bottom line is that the duration of the Babylonian Captivity was a theological construct first and a chronological measurement second, and the biblical witnesses themselves can't agree on the number. Take your pick — and notice that no historical reading lands you at 70 exact years anyway.

entries.question: Will Ephraim return to Egypt?
entries.summary: Hosea 8:13 and 9:3 announce that Ephraim — the northern kingdom — will return to Egypt as punishment. Hosea 11:5 declares that Ephraim shall not return into the land of Egypt, but rather the Assyrian will be his king. The contradiction is internal to a single prophet, and the prophet doesn't seem to notice the problem.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner intra-book contradictions in the prophetic literature. Two declarations, three chapters apart, both attributed to the prophet Hosea, both about the same nation, both predicting opposite outcomes. Hosea 8:13 — mitsrayim yashuvu, 'to Egypt they shall return' — and 9:3 — Ephraim shall return to Egypt and eat unclean things in Assyria — versus 11:5 — lo' yashuv el-erets mitsrayim, 'he shall not return to the land of Egypt,' but Assyria shall be his king.

The critical commentators have generally taken one of three approaches. Approach one: the verses come from different compositional layers, and the contradiction reflects different prophetic moments preserved in the redacted book. Hans Walter Wolff in the Hermeneia Hosea reads 8:13/9:3 as early Hosean material from the period before the Assyrian deportation, when 'return to Egypt' was still a live political possibility, and 11:5 as later material reflecting the actual Assyrian conquest. Approach two: 'Egypt' in Hosea is functioning as a theological symbol for slavery and judgment, not always a literal geographic destination. Francis Andersen and David Noel Freedman in the AB Hosea make a version of this case, reading 'return to Egypt' as a shorthand for reversal of the Exodus, with Assyria as the actual destination. Approach three: the verses are addressing different sub-groups within Ephraim, with some refugees fleeing to Egypt and others deported to Assyria. James Mays in the OTL Hosea entertains this option.

Each approach has some merit, but each comes at a cost. Approach one is the most historically respectable but concedes the contradiction is real — it just attributes it to redaction. Approach two requires reading 8:13 and 9:3 metaphorically while reading 11:5 literally, which is a directionality the text doesn't signal. Approach three has slight historical support — Jeremiah 41-44 records actual Judean refugees fleeing to Egypt after the fall of Jerusalem, and there's no reason a similar thing couldn't have happened with northerners — but the verses themselves don't make that subgroup distinction.

The simplest critical reading is Wolff's redaction-history one. The book of Hosea was composed across decades during the lead-up to and aftermath of the Assyrian destruction of the northern kingdom in 722 BCE, and the prophet's predictions about Egypt got modified as actual political events unfolded. The 'will Ephraim return to Egypt' question doesn't have a single answer in Hosea because the book is a compilation of oracles delivered at different historical moments under different political assumptions. The contradiction is genuine, and trying to harmonize it without acknowledging compositional history requires you to allegorize verses the prophet probably meant literally.
